subject: English
title: Priya and Rohan's Market Adventure
hook: Learn to read and understand short stories about everyday friends and families.

slides.title: Reading Comprehension
slides.storyContext: Priya and Rohan learn to read and understand stories about people, places, and fun things.

slides.title: At the Market
slides.storyContext: Priya and Rohan go to the market with Priya's mama. They see colourful fruits, vegetables, and happy shopkeepers. Read along as they discover new words and ideas.

slides.title: Priya Finds Her Friend
slides.storyContext: At the market, Priya sees Rohan standing near the fruit stall. 'Hello, Rohan!' she shouts happily. Rohan waves. They decide to explore the market together with Mama. Mama holds their hands as they walk past the vegetables and flowers.

points.text: This is the beginning of our story. We meet the characters.
The setting is the market — a busy place with many shoppers.

slides.title: Who, What, and Where?

points.label: Who
points.text: Identify the characters in the story — people, animals, or objects that do things.

points.label: What
points.text: Find out what happens — the action or event in the story.

points.label: Where
points.text: Notice where the story takes place — home, school, market, park.

example.problem: Story: Priya sees red apples at the market. Question: Where does Priya see the apples?
example.solution: Answer: At the market.

slides.inSimpleWords: When we read, we ask: Who is in the story? What do they do? Where does it happen?

slides.title: Finding Who, What, and Where
slides.storyContext: Let's practice with Priya and Rohan's story.

example.problem: Priya and Rohan walk with Mama. They stop at the apple stall. Rohan picks a big red apple. 'This is sweet!' he says.
example.solution: Who: Priya, Rohan, and Mama. What: They walk, stop, pick an apple, and say it is sweet. Where: At the market, at the apple stall.

slides.inSimpleWords: Look for the people (who), the action (what), and the place (where).

slides.title: Picture and Words Work Together

points.text: Look at pictures in the book to help you understand the story.
Pictures show you what the words mean.
Pictures make stories more fun and clear.

example.problem: You see a picture of a child eating mango. The words say: 'Aman eats a mango.' What does Aman eat?
example.solution: Answer: A mango. The picture helps you know this.

slides.inSimpleWords: Pictures are like helpers that show you what the story is about.

slides.title: The Shopkeeper's Smile
slides.storyContext: Mama buys tomatoes from a kind shopkeeper. The shopkeeper smiles and gives Priya and Rohan free mangoes. 'Thank you, Uncle!' they say together. The shopkeeper nods happily. 'Good children get treats,' he says with a big smile.

points.text: The shopkeeper is kind and generous.
Priya and Rohan are polite and grateful.

slides.title: Reading Order Words

points.text: First: the beginning of the story.
Next: what happens in the middle.
Last: how the story ends.

example.problem: Story: First, Rohan wakes up. Next, he eats breakfast. Last, he goes to school. What does Rohan do first?
example.solution: Answer: Rohan wakes up first.

slides.inSimpleWords: Stories happen in order: first, next, last. This order helps us understand what happened when.

slides.title: Order in Priya's Day
slides.storyContext: Let's see what happens in the correct order.

example.problem: First, Priya and Mama go to the market. Next, they meet Rohan. Last, the shopkeeper gives them mangoes. Tell the story in order.
example.solution: First: Priya and Mama go to the market. Next: They meet Rohan there. Last: A shopkeeper gives them mangoes. This is the correct order of the story.

slides.inSimpleWords: When we know the order, the story makes sense.

slides.title: Feeling Words in Stories

points.text: Happy, sad, scared, surprised — these are feelings.
Stories tell us how characters feel.
We can feel the same way when we read.

example.problem: Story: Priya finds her lost toy. She smiles and jumps. How does Priya feel?
example.solution: Answer: Priya is happy. We know because she smiles and jumps.

slides.inSimpleWords: When we read, we notice how the people in the story feel — happy, sad, or scared.

slides.title: A Funny Moment at the Market
slides.storyContext: Rohan sees a big pumpkin and laughs. 'This is as big as a ball!' he says. Priya giggles too. Mama smiles at them. 'Come, let's go home. We have many good things to cook,' says Mama. Both children are happy and excited.

points.text: Rohan finds something funny about the pumpkin.
Priya and Mama feel happy too.

slides.title: What Feelings Do They Have?
slides.storyContext: Find the feelings in the story.

example.problem: Priya is excited to go to the market. Rohan is happy to see Priya. Mama is proud of her children. Find three feelings in this story.
example.solution: Feeling 1: Priya is EXCITED. Feeling 2: Rohan is HAPPY. Feeling 3: Mama is PROUD. The story shows us how everyone feels through their words and actions.

slides.inSimpleWords: Look for feeling words and actions that show how characters feel.

slides.title: Find the Main Idea

points.text: The main idea is the big thing the story is about.
It is not one small detail — it is what the whole story teaches.
Ask: What is this story really telling me?

example.problem: Story: Rohan helps his friend. He picks up her books. He shares his lunch. What is this story really about?
example.solution: Answer: The story is about helping a friend. That is the main idea.

slides.inSimpleWords: The main idea is the big message of the story, not just one small thing that happened.

slides.title: The Lesson Priya Learns
slides.storyContext: At home, Priya thinks about her day at the market. She learned new words like 'vegetable' and 'shopkeeper'. She learned that shopping is a real adventure when you have friends and family with you. 'Mama, I had so much fun!' says Priya. Mama hugs her. That night, Priya dreams about the colourful market.

points.text: Priya learned new words and had fun.
Family and friends make everyday things special.

slides.title: What Is the Main Idea?
slides.storyContext: Let's find the main idea of Priya's story.

example.problem: Priya goes to the market with Rohan and Mama. They see many things. They buy fruits and vegetables. The shopkeeper is kind. They have fun together. What is the main idea?
example.solution: The main idea is: A trip to the market with friends and family is fun and teaches you new things. The details (fruits, shopkeeper, etc.) all support this big idea.

slides.inSimpleWords: The main idea is like the heart of the story — the most important thing it teaches us.

slides.title: Rohan's Notebook
slides.storyContext: After the market trip, Rohan writes in his notebook. He draws the apple stall. He writes: 'The market is busy and colourful. Priya is my best friend. Mama is kind. I like going to the market.' He is using what he learned to tell the story again.

points.text: Rohan remembers details from the story.
He retells the story in his own way.

slides.title: Read This Short Story
slides.storyContext: Read this real story and find the answers.

example.problem: Anya goes to her grandmother's house. She sees a garden with red flowers and green plants. Her grandmother is watering the plants. 'Come, Anya,' says Grandmother. 'Let us water the flowers together.' Anya is happy. She helps water the plants.
example.solution: Questions: 1) Who is the main character? Answer: Anya. 2) Where is she? Answer: At her grandmother's house. 3) What does she do? Answer: She waters plants with her grandmother. 4) How does Anya feel? Answer: Happy.

slides.title: Rohan's Practice
slides.storyContext: Rohan goes home and reads his own story about the market. He reads slowly and carefully. He asks himself: Who? What? Where? Why? He draws pictures of what he read. By doing this, he becomes a better reader every day.

points.text: Practice helps you become a better reader.
Ask questions about every story you read.

slides.title: How to Remember What You Read

points.text: Read slowly and think about the words.
Ask yourself: Who, What, Where, Why, How?
Draw pictures or tell the story to a friend.
This helps you remember the story.

example.problem: You read a story and forget what it was about. How can you remember it?
example.solution: Read it again slowly. Ask questions about the characters and what they do. Draw the story or tell it to someone. These ways help your brain remember.

slides.inSimpleWords: Reading slowly, asking questions, and drawing pictures are ways to remember stories better.

slides.title: Practice Reading a New Story
slides.storyContext: Let's read a new story together with these skills.

example.problem: Vikram and Isha go to the park. They play on the swings. They run in the grass. A dog comes to play with them. The dog is brown and friendly. They play until it is time to go home.
example.solution: 1) Who: Vikram, Isha, and a dog. 2) What: They play on swings, run, and play with a dog. 3) Where: In a park. 4) Feelings: Happy and excited. 5) Main idea: Friends and pets make playtime fun.

slides.inSimpleWords: Using these reading skills, you can understand any story.

slides.title: Story Details Help You Understand Better

points.text: Details are small pieces of information in the story.
Examples: The apple is red. The boy is seven years old. The house is big.
Details make the story clear and fun.

example.problem: Story: A girl plays with a red ball in the sunny park. Which details make this story clear?
example.solution: Details: red (colour), ball (what she plays with), sunny (how the weather is), park (where). These details paint a clear picture.

slides.inSimpleWords: Details are the small things that make a story interesting and clear.

slides.title: Priya Reads to Mama
slides.storyContext: Priya reads a simple story to Mama. Mama listens carefully. When Priya finishes, Mama asks questions. 'Who was the main character?' 'What did they do?' Priya answers all the questions. She is becoming a better reader and thinker.

points.text: Priya practices her reading skills.
Mama helps her think about the story.

slides.title: Your Turn to Read and Answer
slides.storyContext: Read this story and find the answers in your workbook.

example.problem: Ravi and his sister Diya play cricket in the park. Diya hits the ball very far. 'Wow!' says Ravi. 'You are good!' Diya laughs. They play until the sun goes down. Then they go home happy and tired.
example.solution: 1) Who are the characters? Answer: Ravi and Diya. 2) What do they do? Answer: They play cricket. 3) Where do they play? Answer: In the park. 4) How do they feel at the end? Answer: Happy and tired.

slides.title: Create Your Own Story Questions
slides.storyContext: Read a short story and write three questions about it.

example.problem: Story: Arjun finds a kitten under a tree. It is small and scared. He gives it milk and a warm blanket. The kitten becomes his pet. Write three questions about this story.
example.solution: Question 1: Who found the kitten? Question 2: Where was the kitten? Question 3: What did Arjun give the kitten? (Your own questions can be different — as long as they ask about the story.)

slides.inSimpleWords: Good readers ask questions about stories. Now YOU create questions too!

slides.title: Why Stories Matter

points.text: Stories teach us new things.
Stories help us understand people and their feelings.
Stories are fun and make us imagine new worlds.

example.problem: Why should we read stories?
example.solution: Stories teach us kindness, friendship, and courage. When we read, we learn about different people and places. Stories make our brains smart and happy.

slides.inSimpleWords: Stories are gifts of knowledge, feelings, and fun.

slides.title: What We Learned Today

points.text: Read stories about people, places, and things we know.
Ask Who, What, and Where to understand the story.
Pictures help us understand words.
Stories happen in order: first, next, last.
Notice feelings: happy, sad, scared.
Find the main idea — what is the story really about?
Practice reading to become better every day.

slides.inSimpleWords: Good readers ask questions and think about what they read. You are becoming a great reader!

subject: English
title: Arjun's Sentence Adventures
hook: Write simple sentences about friends, families, and fun things you love.

slides.title: Simple Writing
slides.storyContext: Arjun learns to write simple, clear sentences about his life and the people he loves.

slides.title: Arjun Wants to Write
slides.storyContext: Arjun goes to Teacher Aunty. 'I want to write a story,' he says. 'But how do I start?' Teacher Aunty smiles. 'We will make it easy. First, we write simple sentences.'

image.alt: Arjun Wants to Write — Simple Writing

slides.title: Teacher Aunty's Magic Words
slides.storyContext: Teacher Aunty shows Arjun her notebook. 'Look,' she says. 'Every good sentence needs two things: someone (or something) and what they do. That is the magic!' Arjun nods. He takes his pencil and listens carefully.

points.text: Teacher Aunty teaches Arjun the secret of writing.
Arjun is excited to learn.

slides.title: A Sentence Has a Subject and an Action

points.label: Subject
points.text: The person or thing the sentence is about (who or what).

points.label: Action
points.text: What the subject does (the verb).

example.problem: Write a sentence about Saya doing something. Use: Saya + an action.
example.solution: Saya plays football. (Subject: Saya. Action: plays.)

slides.inSimpleWords: Every sentence needs someone or something (the subject) and something they do (the action).

slides.title: Finding Subject and Action
slides.storyContext: Let's find subjects and actions in Arjun's sentences.

example.problem: Sentence: Arjun writes in his notebook. Find: What is the subject? What is the action?
example.solution: Subject: Arjun (the person). Action: writes (what he does). A complete sentence needs both!

slides.inSimpleWords: The subject is WHO. The action is WHAT they do. Together they make a sentence.

slides.title: Use Capital Letters and Full Stops

points.text: Start every sentence with a capital letter.
End every sentence with a full stop (.).
Capital letters show that a sentence is starting.

example.problem: Fix this: arjun is a good boy. Answer: Arjun is a good boy.
example.solution: We start with a capital A. We end with a full stop. Now it is correct!

slides.inSimpleWords: Sentences start big (capital letter) and end with a dot (full stop).

slides.title: Arjun's First Sentences
slides.storyContext: Arjun writes: 'I love to play. My friend Saya is kind. Teacher Aunty helps me learn.' He shows Teacher Aunty. 'Very good!' she says with a big smile. 'Every sentence starts big and ends with a dot. You are a writer!'

points.text: Arjun writes three simple sentences.
Teacher Aunty praises him.

slides.title: Describing Words Make Sentences Better

points.text: Describing words tell us more about nouns.
Examples: big, small, red, happy, quick, slow, beautiful.
Describing words help readers picture the story.

example.problem: Sentence: Saya has an apple. Make it better with a describing word.
example.solution: Saya has a red apple. Or: Saya has a big apple. The describing word makes it clearer!

slides.inSimpleWords: Describing words help us see and feel the story better. They paint a picture with words.

slides.title: Adding Describing Words
slides.storyContext: Let's make Arjun's sentences more interesting.

example.problem: Simple: I have a notebook. Better: I have a blue notebook. Better still: I have a big blue notebook.
example.solution: Adding describing words (blue, big) makes your sentence more interesting and clear. Readers can picture it better!

slides.inSimpleWords: Describing words make your writing beautiful and clear.

slides.title: Write About Things You Know

points.text: Write about your family, friends, home, school.
Write about things you do every day.
Write about your feelings and your favourite things.

example.problem: Write a sentence about your favourite food from home.
example.solution: My mother makes tasty dal and rice. Or: I like sweet ladoos. Write what you really know and like!

slides.inSimpleWords: The best stories come from your own life. Write what you know.

slides.title: Saya's Writing Too
slides.storyContext: Saya also learns to write. She writes: 'My family loves me. I play with Arjun. We read together.' Teacher Aunty says both children are becoming writers. 'Keep writing,' she tells them. 'Every day, you grow better.'

points.text: Saya writes about her life and family.
Practice helps both children improve.

slides.title: Sentences Tell Complete Thoughts

points.text: A sentence is a complete thought. It makes sense on its own.
Incomplete: 'The big dog.' (What about the dog?)
Complete: 'The big dog runs fast.' (Now we know what it does.)

example.problem: Is this a complete sentence? 'Ravi in the garden.' Answer: No. Make it complete.
example.solution: Ravi plays in the garden. Now it is complete and makes sense.

slides.inSimpleWords: A good sentence tells a complete thought. Read it and ask: Does it make sense?

slides.title: Complete vs Incomplete
slides.storyContext: Let's learn the difference.

example.problem: Incomplete: 'The sweet'. Complete: 'I eat the sweet.' Can you see the difference?
example.solution: Incomplete does not tell us what is happening. Complete tells us who does what. Always write complete sentences.

slides.inSimpleWords: Every sentence must answer: Who? What do they do? Then it is complete.

slides.title: Putting Sentences Together

points.text: When you write two or more sentences, they tell a bigger story.
Example: 'I wake up. I eat breakfast. I go to school.'
These sentences work together to paint a picture.

example.problem: Write three sentences about your morning.
example.solution: Example: I wake up early. I eat tasty food. I get ready for school. These three sentences tell the story of your morning.

slides.inSimpleWords: Many sentences together tell a whole story.

slides.title: Write Your Own Sentences
slides.storyContext: Here are real sentence examples about friends and school.

example.problem: Write three sentences about your best friend or your school day.
example.solution: Example 1: My friend Isha is kind and smart. Example 2: We play together in the park. Example 3: I like being with Isha.

slides.title: Writing Contest at School
slides.storyContext: Teacher Aunty announces a writing contest. 'Who can write the best sentences?' she asks. Arjun and Saya both want to try. They practice every day. They write about their pets, their families, and their dreams. Soon, they have many wonderful sentences.

points.text: Arjun and Saya practice writing often.
They write about things they love.

slides.title: Write a Short Paragraph
slides.storyContext: Now write 3–4 simple sentences about something you did today.

example.problem: Write a short paragraph: What did you do today? Use complete sentences. Start with capital letters. End with full stops.
example.solution: Example: Today I went to school. My teacher taught us about animals. I drew a picture of a tiger. Then I played with my friends. This is a short paragraph — 4 complete sentences about one day.

slides.title: Fix the Sentences
slides.storyContext: These sentences have mistakes. Can you fix them?

example.problem: 1) saya is my friend 2) I like to play. he is nice. 3) we go to school. Fix each one.
example.solution: 1) Saya is my friend. 2) I like to play. He is nice. 3) We go to school. (Start with capital letters, end with full stops.)

slides.inSimpleWords: Always check: Does my sentence start big and end with a dot?

slides.title: Your Writing Voice

points.text: Write in your own way, with your own words.
Do not copy. Tell your own story.
Your words are special and unique.

example.problem: Two children write about their pet. Their sentences are different. Is that okay?
example.solution: Yes! Every person writes in their own way. That is good. Your writing is YOUR voice.

slides.inSimpleWords: Write what YOU think and feel. Your words are special.

slides.title: Arjun and Saya's Contest
slides.storyContext: On contest day, Arjun and Saya read their work to the whole class. Arjun writes about his puppy. Saya writes about her grandmother. Teacher Aunty and all the students clap for them. Both children feel proud. 'You are both winners,' says Teacher Aunty, 'because you tried your best.'

points.text: Both children participate in the contest.
Effort and practice matter most.

slides.title: How to Start Writing

points.text: Think of something you know or love.
Decide on a subject — who or what you will write about.
Write your subject, then the action — it becomes your first sentence!

example.problem: You want to write about your school. How do you start?
example.solution: Think: My school is my subject. Action: I learn and play there. Sentence: I learn and play at my school.

slides.inSimpleWords: Start by thinking of a subject. Add an action. Boom — you have a sentence!

slides.title: Checking Your Writing

points.text: After you write, read it again slowly.
Ask: Does it make sense? Does it have a subject and action?
Check: Does it start with a capital letter and end with a full stop?

example.problem: You wrote: 'my dog is brown.' How do you check it?
example.solution: Read it. Subject: my dog. Action: is brown. Good! Now check capitals and full stops. Fix: 'My dog is brown.' Perfect!

slides.inSimpleWords: Always check your work before showing it to someone.

slides.title: Writing Tips to Remember

points.text: A sentence has a subject (who or what) and an action (what they do).
Start with a capital letter. End with a full stop.
Use describing words to paint a picture.
Write about things you know and love.
Make sure your sentence is complete and makes sense.
Write in your own voice and be proud of your writing!

slides.inSimpleWords: You are a writer now! Write simple, clear sentences about your life. Every day, you will get better.

subject: English
title: Maya's Word Treasure Hunt
hook: Discover new words and learn what they mean through fun stories and pictures.

slides.title: Words and Meanings
slides.storyContext: Maya and Vikram hunt for new words. Grandmother teaches them real, everyday words from stories.

image.alt: Words and Meanings — Words and Meanings

slides.title: The Word Treasure Hunt Begins
slides.storyContext: Maya and Vikram sit with Grandmother in the garden. 'Grandmother, can you teach us new words?' asks Maya. Grandmother nods. 'Of course! The world is full of beautiful words. Let us find them together.'

image.alt: The Word Treasure Hunt Begins — Words and Meanings

slides.title: Grandmother's Word Game
slides.storyContext: Grandmother shows them a book with bright pictures. 'Look at this picture,' she says, pointing to a garden. 'What do you see?' 'Flowers!' cries Vikram. 'Garden!' says Maya. 'Yes! These are words. Each word stands for something we see and know.'

points.text: Words are names for things we see.
Pictures help us learn words.

slides.title: Every Word Has a Meaning

points.text: A word is a sound or group of letters that stands for something.
The meaning is what the word tells us.
Pictures, stories, and examples help us learn meanings.

example.problem: Word: GARDEN. What does garden mean?
example.solution: A garden is a place where plants and flowers grow. It can have vegetables, flowers, or trees. Grandmother's garden has bright flowers.

slides.inSimpleWords: A word is like a name for something. The meaning tells us what that something is.

slides.title: Learning Words From Pictures
slides.storyContext: Let's practice with Grandmother's pictures.

example.problem: Show a picture of a mango. The word is MANGO. What does it mean?
example.solution: A mango is a fruit. It is sweet and yellow or orange when ripe. We eat mangoes in summer. The picture shows what a mango looks like.

slides.inSimpleWords: Pictures show us what words mean. Words name the things we see.

slides.title: Rhyming Words Sound the Same at the End

points.text: Rhyming words end with the same sound.
Examples: cat and hat, run and fun, day and play.
Rhymes make stories fun to read and remember.

example.problem: Find a word that rhymes with 'ball'. Answer choices: wall, food, tree.
example.solution: Answer: wall. Ball and wall rhyme because they end with the same sound: -all.

slides.inSimpleWords: Rhyming words are like sound friends. They sound alike at the end.

slides.title: Maya Finds Rhymes
slides.storyContext: Maya plays with sounds. 'Cat, hat, sat!' she sings. 'They rhyme!' Grandmother smiles. 'Yes! Listen to how they sound alike. Rhyming words are fun to say. They help us remember stories.'

points.text: Maya discovers rhyming words.
Rhymes make words fun.

slides.title: Opposite Words

points.label: Opposites
points.text: Words that mean completely different things.
Examples: big and small, hot and cold, happy and sad.
Opposites help us describe things better.

example.problem: Opposite of 'tall'. Answer choices: short, fast, red.
example.solution: Answer: short. Tall and short are opposites. Tall means big up-down. Short means not big up-down.

slides.inSimpleWords: Opposite words are like two ends of a line. They mean different things.

slides.title: Finding Opposite Pairs
slides.storyContext: Let's find opposite words.

example.problem: Find the opposite: Big, Happy, Fast, Hot. Opposites: small, sad, slow, cold.
example.solution: Big opposite is SMALL. Happy opposite is SAD. Fast opposite is SLOW. Hot opposite is COLD. Can you say why they are opposites?

slides.inSimpleWords: Opposites describe two different ends of something.

slides.title: Words That Sound the Same But Mean Different Things

points.text: Some words sound the same but mean different things.
Example: 'sun' (in the sky) and 'son' (a boy child). Both sound like 'sun'.
We learn which is which from the sentence around it.

example.problem: Vikram sees the sun. The sun is bright and warm. Does this 'sun' mean a boy child? Answer: No.
example.solution: 'Sun' here means the star in the sky, not a boy child (son). The sentence tells us it is bright and warm. That helps us know which word it is.

slides.inSimpleWords: Some words sound the same but mean different things. The sentence helps us know which one.

slides.title: Vikram Gets Confused
slides.storyContext: Vikram reads: 'The baker's son made bread.' Vikram laughs. 'Is this about the sun in the sky making bread?' Grandmother says, 'No! Listen: S-O-N, not S-U-N. Son means a boy child. Sun means the bright star. The sentence helps us know which one!'

points.text: Words that sound alike can have different meanings.
The rest of the sentence helps us understand.

slides.title: New Words From Stories

points.text: When you read, you find new words you do not know.
Look at the story and pictures for clues.
Ask yourself: 'What does this word do in the story?'

example.problem: Story: 'The merchant sold silk in the market.' What might 'merchant' mean?
example.solution: A merchant is a person who sells things. The story says the merchant sold silk in the market. We learned the meaning from the story!

slides.inSimpleWords: When you meet a new word, look at the story for clues. The story helps you understand.

slides.title: Real Words From Everyday Life
slides.storyContext: Here are real words Maya and Vikram learned from Grandmother.

example.problem: Learn these words: FESTIVAL (a big celebration with music and food), MONSOON (season of heavy rain), BAZAAR (a busy market), LANTERN (a light that can move).
example.solution: Festival: Diwali is a big festival with lights and sweets. Monsoon: In monsoon, it rains hard for many days. Bazaar: We buy vegetables in the bazaar. Lantern: Grandmother lit a lantern when the lights went out.

slides.title: Using New Words
slides.storyContext: Maya says, 'During monsoon, we stay inside. But I love it because the earth smells fresh. The bazaar becomes very crowded. At night, Grandmother uses her old lantern to tell stories during festivals.'

points.text: Maya uses new words in her own sentences.
New words make her writing rich and beautiful.

slides.title: How to Find Meaning When You Are Stuck

points.text: Read the sentence again slowly.
Look at pictures near the word.
Ask yourself: What does this word do? What does it describe?
Ask a friend or adult if you are still stuck.

example.problem: Unknown word: LUMINOUS. Sentence: 'The luminous stars shone at night.' What might it mean?
example.solution: The word is about stars. Stars shine. Luminous probably means bright or shining. (Yes! Luminous means giving off light.)

slides.inSimpleWords: When you find a new word, use clues from the sentence to guess its meaning.

slides.title: Find the Meaning
slides.storyContext: Read and find the right meaning.

example.problem: Word: BRAVE. Choose the meaning: (1) scared and worried, (2) not scared and facing danger, (3) alone and sad. What is the meaning of BRAVE?
example.solution: Answer: (2) not scared and facing danger. Vikram is brave when he helps his friend even when he is worried. Brave means you do something even if it is hard.

slides.title: Make Your Own Sentences With New Words
slides.storyContext: Use the new words you learned to make sentences.

example.problem: Use these words to make sentences: FESTIVAL, MONSOON, BAZAAR. Make sure your sentences make sense.
example.solution: Example 1: I love going to the bazaar with my mother. Example 2: During monsoon, the plants grow very green. Example 3: We celebrate the festival with lights and music. Your sentences should show you understand the meaning.

slides.inSimpleWords: When you use new words in your own sentences, you really learn them!

slides.title: Grandmother's Word Gift
slides.storyContext: At the end of the week, Grandmother gives Maya and Vikram a special gift — a notebook. 'Write new words here,' she says. 'Draw pictures next to them. One day, this notebook will be full of treasures.' Both children smile. They have learned so much!

points.text: Grandmother encourages them to keep learning.
Collecting new words is like finding treasure.

slides.title: Building Your Word Treasure

points.text: Every new word you learn is a treasure.
The more words you know, the better you can read and write.
Keep finding new words everywhere — in stories, at home, in school.

example.problem: How can you build your word treasure?
example.solution: Read every day. Ask about new words. Use them in sentences. Write them down. Soon you will have many beautiful words!

slides.inSimpleWords: Words are like jewels — collect them and make your writing shine.

slides.title: Sharing Words With Friends

points.text: When you learn a new word, tell your friends!
Teaching others helps you remember better.
Friends can help you learn new words too.

example.problem: You learned a new word: SERENE (peaceful and calm). How do you teach it?
example.solution: Tell your friend: 'Serene means peaceful. The quiet garden is serene. It makes me feel calm.' Now your friend knows the word too!

slides.inSimpleWords: Sharing words makes learning fun for everyone.

slides.title: Words Are Everywhere

points.text: Every word has a meaning that tells us what it is.
Rhyming words sound the same at the end.
Opposite words mean different things.
Some words sound the same but mean different things.
Stories and pictures help us learn new word meanings.
Keep learning new words every day!

slides.inSimpleWords: Words are treasures. The more words you know, the more stories you can read and the more you can write.
